query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles, the chemical complexity leads to a kinetically trapped, uniformly mixed solid solution with severely restricted atomic mobility. This kinetic constraint delays the onset of localized pre‐melting (surface diffusion or segregation) and forces a more abrupt, higher-temperature melting transition compared to simpler (bimetallic or single‐metal) nanoparticles.
generation.material_initial_state: Initially solid, single-phase nanoparticles of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu configured as a random solid solution.
generation.intervention: Heat the HEA nanoparticles at a controlled rate through the premelting and melting regime, and compare their phase-transition behavior with that of similarly sized bimetallic (or single‐metal) nanoparticles processed under identical thermal conditions.
generation.conditions: Use identical, well-controlled thermal ramp conditions (e.g., defined heating rate in an inert atmosphere) and nanoparticle size distributions that ensure limited atomic mobility (solid precursor state). Measurements (via in-situ DSC, TEM, or other temperature‐dependent techniques) should be performed below the boiling/vaporization range of the constituent metals.
generation.structural_mediator: The high configurational entropy and the dilution of specific atomic pair interactions limit the free mobility of individual atoms within the solid nanoparticle, thereby mediating the phase evolution.
generation.mechanism: Because the atoms in the multi-element solid solution are both more dilute (reducing strong pairwise interactions) and confined by the solid precursor’s limited mobility, the energetically favorable pathways for gradual surface premelting and atomic segregation are suppressed. This kinetic trapping forces the nanoparticle to retain its homogeneous structure until a critical temperature is reached, at which point a rapid and more synchronized melting occurs.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to bimetallic or pure-metal nanoparticles undergoing the same thermal treatment, the HEA nanoparticles will show (a) a delayed premelting onset, (b) a sharper melting transition occurring at a somewhat higher temperature relative to the baseline, and (c) minimal pre-melting phase segregation or local ordering.
generation.baseline: Identically sized bimetallic or single‐metal nanoparticles that exhibit earlier onset of surface premelting and gradual phase segregation prior to full melting.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to nanoparticles synthesized from a solid mixed-precursor (with limited free atomic mobility) in the size regime where diffusion is kinetically restrained and for temperature conditions below the vaporization/boiling ranges of the constituent metals.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature shifts and magnitude of the delayed premelting interval are uncertain and depend on factors such as nanoparticle size distribution, heating rate, and minor variations in composition. Quantitative differences need to be established experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of nanoparticles: (i) Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu HEA nanoparticles and (ii) a control set such as bimetallic (e.g., Fe–Ni) nanoparticles of similar sizes. Subject both sets to identical heating protocols (using in-situ DSC and TEM) across the premelting and melting regimes.
measurements: DSC thermograms to determine the onset temperatures and sharpness of transitions
In-situ TEM to observe the evolution of morphology and any phase segregation during heating
EDS or other elemental mapping to check for uniformity vs. segregation prior to and during melting
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the HEA nanoparticles display either (a) an earlier or more gradual premelting onset comparable to or less abrupt than the bimetallic particles, (b) significant elemental segregation or the formation of separate phases during heating prior to melting, or (c) no distinguishable difference in melting behavior relative to simpler nanoparticles.

This behavior contrasts with the bimetallic case, suggesting that the rules governing phase formation differ for the systems containing two or five elements: Single-phase alloy formation occurs more readily if more elements are present, as systems that are immiscible on the bimetallic level can be driven to mix by introducing more elements. As the resulting phases of the binary particles cannot readily be explained by their thermodynamic stability, we devised a kinetic model to rationalize the experimental results based on the restrictions imposed by the synthesis. When comparing five-element and two-element mixtures, the concentration of individual atom types is reduced the more elements are present. This will make it increasingly difficult for elements with strong preferences of ordering to form an intermetallic structure or for elements that repulse each other to segregate, simply because they are more dilute. Simultaneous in situ X-ray diffraction and multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy experiments allowed us to study the formation mechanism of noble metal bimetallic and high entropy alloy nanoparticles in depth. The samples were prepared by reduction of single-source precursors. For five-element mixtures, the formation of a single phase occurs more readily than in the binary samples. Under the studied reaction conditions, single-phase formation for binary alloys was restricted to systems where cooperative reduction occurred, while single-phase HEA particles could be obtained even though the elements were reduced consecutively. The findings are explained with a stochastic model that simulates the particle formation process. Regardless of the element interactions, the model quantifies that it is more likely to form a random alloy if more atom types are present in a system with limited free atom mobility. This highlights that knowledge of the formation mechanism is crucial for understanding the material formation pathways.
